title: Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques: Promising Directions From Cognitive and Educational Psychology https://pcl.sitehost.iu.edu/rgoldsto/courses/dunloskyimprovinglearning.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), January 17, 2025 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarises the full Dunlosky et al. monograph, the longer, more rigorous companion to Strengthening the Student Toolbox, which rates ten learning techniques as high, moderate, or low utility based on how robustly and broadly their benefits generalise. Practice testing and distributed practice again earn high utility ratings for benefiting learners of different ages and abilities across many contexts; elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, and interleaved practice earn moderate; and summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonics, imagery, and rereading are rated low utility. Barton draws out the monograph's diagnosis that many teachers simply aren't informed about which techniques actually work, and its concrete classroom suggestions, such as opening new units with a practice test on the previous section, interleaving related problems across units, and explanatory why questioning when introducing key concepts, as ways to build these into ordinary lesson planning rather than treating them as add-ons.
points: Practice testing and distributed practice are the only two techniques rated high utility, meaning their benefits are robust and generalise widely across ages, abilities, and materials.
Interleaved practice, elaborative interrogation, and self-explanation are rated moderate utility — genuinely useful, but with more context-dependent or less-established evidence.
Highlighting, rereading, summarisation, keyword mnemonics, and imagery are rated low utility, meaning teachers and students are often better served using other strategies.
Many teachers are not fully informed about the efficacy of different learning techniques, meaning students may default to popular but low-value strategies like highlighting and rereading.
Concrete lesson-planning suggestions include opening new units with a practice test on the prior section and interleaving recently studied problems with related ones from earlier units.
quotes: The authors review existing research to determine each technique's relative utility, assigning ratings of high, moderate, or low based on the robustness and generalizability of their benefits.
Practice testing has been shown to benefit learners of different ages and abilities and has been shown to boost students' performance across many criterion tasks and in educational contexts.
Distributed practice has also received a high utility assessment because of its broad benefits for learners.
Many teachers are not fully informed about the efficacy of different learning techniques, and as a result, students may not be using effective strategies.
Rereading is a popular technique, but it does not consistently improve students' performance.
Students and teachers who are not already doing so should consider using techniques designated as high utility, because the effects of these techniques are robust and generalize widely
